title: The Marshmallow Test (Mischel; Kidd et al., 2013)

youtube.title: One Marshmallow Now, or Two Later? It's Not Willpower. #Shorts
youtube.description:
You're four. One marshmallow now, or two if you can wait alone in the room.
For decades, waiting was supposed to predict your whole future.

This is Walter Mischel's marshmallow test, told from the inside. A much bigger 2018 study found the link was far smaller than we thought. And a 2013 study showed kids who were let down by an adult waited about 3 minutes, while kids who could trust the adult waited about 12.

Would YOU wait, if you weren't sure the second one was coming? Tell me in the comments.

Sources:
- Mischel, W., Shoda, Y., & Rodriguez, M. L. (1989). Delay of gratification in children. Science, 244.
- Watts, T. W., Duncan, G. J., & Quan, H. (2018). Revisiting the marshmallow test. Psychological Science, 29(7).
- Kidd, C., Palmeri, H., & Aslin, R. N. (2013). Rational snacking. Cognition, 126(1).

#psychology #marshmallowtest #selfcontrol #shorts #mindset

sources: Mischel's studies at Stanford's Bing Nursery School (1960s-70s): one treat now, or two if the child waited alone for the researcher to return; children distracted themselves to wait (Mischel, Shoda & Rodriguez 1989, Science 244).
Follow-ups linked longer waiting to later outcomes such as SAT scores (Shoda, Mischel & Peake 1990).
Watts, Duncan & Quan (2018), Psychological Science 29(7): with about 900 children the link was much smaller and largely explained by family background and early ability.

Kidd, Palmeri & Aslin (2013), Cognition 126(1): after an adult broke a promise of better art supplies, children waited about 3 minutes on average; after a kept promise, about 12 minutes (28 children).
lines: You're four years old. A marshmallow sits on the table in front of you. Eat it now, or wait and get two.
Stanford, the nineteen sixties. The researcher walks out and closes the door. You have no idea when he'll come back.
Some kids eat it in seconds. Others cover their eyes, sing to themselves, or turn their backs on it.
Years later, kids who waited longer seemed to do better, even on school tests. Willpower, it seemed, could predict your future.
But in twenty eighteen, a much bigger study tried again, with about nine hundred kids. The link was far smaller.
Most of it was explained by family background, money and early skills, not just willpower.
Then another study did something sneaky first. An adult promised kids better crayons, and never brought them.
Those let down kids waited about three minutes. Kids whose promise was kept waited about twelve. Four times longer.
Maybe it was never just willpower. Maybe it was trust. Would you wait, if you weren't sure the second one was coming?
